newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Wheat and oil squeezed higher on weather.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wheat and oil squeezed higher on weather.

text.p: Weather conditions provided the driving force for world commodity markets on Monday as wheat and oil prices moved sharply higher on supply concerns.

Other commodity markets saw coffee retreat from the day's gains on profit-taking after a firm start on last week's rally and continuing strike worries in Colombia. Soybean and corn futures were seen lifted by gains in wheat.

Chicago Board of Trade soft red winter wheat futures soared in early Chicago trading as traders said severe flooding along the Red River in the Northern U.S. Plains could mean that much of the spring wheat acreage is abandoned.

Approximately 1.7 million acres of North Dakota cropland were under water due to flooding and much of that acreage will not go into agricultural production this growing season, North Dakota Congressman Earl Pomeroy said on Sunday.
Concern over the damage done by a weekend freeze in the U.S. Great Plains boosted wheat futures last week and continued to do so on Monday as the extent of the damage was still not yet fully known.

Meanwhile, drought conditions in Europe persisted and farm industry sources said lack of rain in eastern England may be causing real damage to the developing grains crop. Traders in Spain said the Spanish cereal crop could be reduced by around 15 percent due to lack of rain.
CBOT soft red winter wheat futures for May rose eight cents to trade just off the day's highs at $4.45 a bushel in London's Monday afternoon.

World oil prices were also boosted by weather reports, which forecast a cold snap in the United States. Independent forecasters Weather Services Corp said temperatures in the United States were likely to remain below normal over the next ten days.

News of Iraq's plans to fly through a no-fly zone and further protests by Iranian students against a Berlin court verdict accusing Iran's leaders of ordering political killings also pushed oil prices higher.
Iraq said on Monday it was sending helicopters to pick up returning Moslem pilgrims from the Saudi border despite a ban by the United States and other western powers on Iraqi flights in the area.
The July futures contract for benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil had climbed more than half a dollar in London's afternoon, trading at $18.48 a barrel before coming off slightly.
"It's like the Iraqis are throwing down the gauntlet to the U.S. and they will have to react. That's how the market seems to be reading it anyway," one London broker said.
Coffee futures of the robusta type retreated from the day's gains in London's Monday afternoon, dragged down by choppy fund-led trade in New York.
Coffee prices for arabicas in New York slipped back from fresh contract highs set in early trade as commodity funds swept in to take profits on the rally.
World coffee prices surged last week as a two-day stoppage by port workers in Brazil, the world's largest coffee producer, sparked supply concerns.
Prices shot up again in early Monday trade in New York after the start of a long-planned truckers' strike in Colombia, the world's number two coffee producer, over the weekend.
Gold remained firmly planted within its range between $340 and $345, ending the day barely changed after following platinum upwards early in London, but failing to sustain momentum above $342.
Copper and aluminium saw little action in a day lacking market-moving news.
